claim_verdicts.evidence: how-query-works.md, "When queries are executed": "When you call LINQ operators, you're simply building up an in-memory representation of the query. The query is only sent to the database when the results are consumed." Triggers listed: "Iterating the results in a `for` loop"; "Using an operator such as `ToList`, `ToArray`, `Single`, `Count`, or the equivalent async overloads" — ToListAsync/FirstOrDefaultAsync are such async overloads. Mirror is post-EF10 (single-split-queries.md speaks of "EF versions prior to 10").

how-query-works.md, "The life of a query": "The database provider identifies which parts of the query can be evaluated in the database / These parts of the query are translated to database-specific query language (for example, SQL for a relational database) / A query is sent to the database and the result set returned". That page carries an "out of date" banner, so also confirmed by execution: with log_statement=all on donhang-db, one GET /api/v1/orders produced exactly one prepared statement (setting then reset to none).

single-split-queries.md: "When working against relational databases, EF loads related entities by introducing JOINs into a single query"; splitting is opt-in — "EF allows you to specify that a given LINQ query should be *split* into multiple SQL queries", plus a separate "Enabling split queries globally" section. DonHangDbContext sets no splitting behaviour. Observed SQL: ListByCustomerAsync -> one statement "FROM orders AS o INNER JOIN customers AS c ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.customer_id = $1 ORDER BY o.id"; FindAsync -> one statement with "LEFT JOIN order_items".

`git -C examples/don-hang show stage-1:DonHang.Infrastructure/EfOrderRepository.cs` is 19 lines and diffs clean against the lesson block (lines 1-19, byte-identical). Both queries are expression-bodied: "public Task<Order?> FindAsync(int id) => db.Orders.Include(o => o.Items).FirstOrDefaultAsync(o => o.Id == id);" and "public Task<List<Order>> ListByCustomerAsync(int customerId) => db.Orders.Where(o => o.CustomerId == customerId).Include(o => o.Customer).OrderBy(o => o.Id).ToListAsync();". Only AddAsync uses async/await.

Live run 2026-09-24 against the stage-1 lab (localhost:8080). anh.tran@example.com -> [{id 1 paid},{id 2 shipped},{id 10 paid}] all "Trần Minh Anh"; chau.nguyen@example.com -> [{id 3 paid},{id 4 cancelled},{id 11 shipped}] all "Nguyễn Bảo Châu" — disjoint. OrdersController.List() reads customerId from the token's `sub` claim and calls repository.ListByCustomerAsync(customerId); the postgres log for that request shows WHERE o.customer_id = $1, Parameters: $1 = '1'.

issues.text: Wrong timing, and it contradicts the lesson's own summary line 5. ToListAsync/FirstOrDefaultAsync are async methods: "When you invoke an async method, it runs synchronously until it reaches the first `await` on an incomplete awaitable" (dotnet docs) — the enumeration, and the SQL, start when the call is *made*; awaiting only waits for an already-running Task. Summary line 5 says exactly that ("returns the `Task` its own final call already produces"), so a reader following §4 concludes `var t = q.ToListAsync();` sends nothing until an `await`, which is false.
issues.quote: one SQL statement, built from the whole chain, run only when the last call is awaited
issues.fix: Write "...run only when that last call is made". The same paragraph's earlier wording ("only `.ToListAsync()` — or `.FirstOrDefaultAsync()`, or a `foreach` — does that") is already correct. Leave the Beginners-often-think bullet alone: it quotes the outline's misconception verbatim.

issues.text: Unlisted claim: the lesson's central evidence is a debugger observation stated three times (§2 "find the paused variable holding something with no rows in it at all", here, and §6 "shows no query has run yet") and appears in no claim of .meta.json. It is also IDE-dependent: pausing does not enumerate the queryable, but inspecting it in a debugger view that expands an IQueryable's results does enumerate it and sends the SQL. Nothing in the EF Core 10 docs governs debugger behaviour, so the sentence is asserted without a source.
issues.quote: This is why a breakpoint right after `.Where(...)` sees no database activity
issues.fix: Add the condition and a ledger entry: "...sees no database activity — as long as you only look at the variable, not expand a debugger view that asks the query for its rows". Add a `behavior` claim to .meta.json sourced to the EF Core deferred-execution page plus the note that debugger inspection can itself enumerate.

issues.text: Ambiguous key: distractor c is true as written, so two options answer the question. In EF Core 10 a Where over a DbSet is never client-evaluated — "If EF Core detects an expression, in any place other than the top-level projection, which can't be translated to the server, then it throws a runtime exception" (client-eval.md) — and no Order objects exist when .Where(...) is called. c thus refutes the teammate; its explanation ("This overstates the case: .Where(...) builds a query description, not a filter over objects that already exist") restates c instead of refuting it.
issues.quote: `.Where(...)` cannot run in C# at all, since `Order` objects don't exist yet at the point it's called
issues.fix: Make c false, e.g. "`.Where(...)` has no effect on speed either way, since PostgreSQL ignores the condition and EF Core drops the extra rows after loading them", with explanation "PostgreSQL does apply the condition — the statement it receives ends in `WHERE o.customer_id = ...` — so no extra row is ever loaded." Keep the key at a.

issues.text: Beyond the outline: neither the three outline items nor `depth_notes` concerns C# async idiom, yet summary line 5 spends one of five takeaways on `async`/`await` and `Task` return shape, and §5 teaches it as a general rule ("each is one expression ... and that call's own `Task` is what the method returns directly"). The skill taught is `backend.ef.querying`; the fifth takeaway of a LINQ-translation lesson should not be a method-signature idiom.
issues.quote: 5. Neither `FindAsync` nor `ListByCustomerAsync` uses `async`/`await` — each returns the `Task` its own final call already produces.
issues.fix: Replace summary line 5 with the point the lesson actually argues, e.g. "5. Pausing right after `.Where(...)` shows no query has run yet: the variable holds a description, not rows." In §5, reduce the rule to one clause tied to this block ("each method is a single expression, so the chain's own `Task` is returned directly").

issues.text: `.Include(...)` is not a LINQ call. It is an EF Core extension method (Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore, EntityFrameworkQueryableExtensions), described in the docs as "the `Include` method" for eager loading; it does not exist on `System.Linq` sequences the way `Where`/`OrderBy` do. Calling it "a LINQ call" tells the reader it is the same kind of thing as `Where`, which is exactly the distinction that decides whether it can appear on a plain list.
issues.quote: `.Include(...)` — a LINQ call naming related rows to load in the same query
issues.fix: Write "`.Include(...)` — an EF Core call chained into a LINQ query, naming related rows to load in the same query".

issues.text: Unlisted mapping claims: that `db.Orders` stands for the `orders` table, that `Items` are rows of `order_items`, and that `o.Customer` is the row `o.CustomerId` points at. All three are true — DonHangDbContext.cs @ stage-1 has ToTable("orders"), ToTable("order_items"), HasMany(o => o.Items).WithOne().HasForeignKey(i => i.OrderId), HasOne(o => o.Customer).WithMany().HasForeignKey(o => o.CustomerId) — but that file is neither shown nor listed in `example_files`, and no claim records them.
issues.quote: the order's line-item rows in the related `order_items` table, paired in by the foreign key pointing back at this order
issues.fix: Add one `fact` claim to .meta.json covering the three mappings, source `examples/don-hang @ stage-1: DonHang.Infrastructure/DonHangDbContext.cs (OnModelCreating)`; lesson text unchanged.

issues.text: The "how you notice it" test does not hold as stated: if the `orders` table grows because this customer places more orders, the row count the code receives grows with the table. What stays constant is the count with respect to rows belonging to other customers — which is what the executed statement shows (`WHERE o.customer_id = $1` applied before any row is returned).
issues.quote: the row count your code receives does not grow with the size of the table
issues.fix: Write "the row count your code receives does not grow when other customers' orders are added to the table".
